# Problem Statement — PS-001: The Bengali Edition Gap

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Artifact ID | PS-001 |
| Flow Step | 03 — Define target problem (Phase: Problem Discovery) |
| Owner | PM-001 |
| Upstream inputs | IB-001 (Idea Brief v1.0), IOH-001 (Initial Opportunity Hypothesis v1.0) |
| Reviewers this run | CEO-001, UXR-001 (independent, post-production) |
| Version | 3.0 (attempt 3 — supersedes v1.0, v2.0; both returned) |
| Status | Draft → for review |
| Overall confidence | **Medium** |
| Evidence quality | **Low** (no primary research or web/CRM access in this run — see §8) |
| Gate criteria | **MET on specificity, measurability, and outcome-linkage; NOT MET on empirical validation** — §9 is the pre-registered protocol that closes it |

---

## 0. Why this attempt differs from the two that were returned

The prior attempts were returned for low confidence on an evidence-led step. Restating the same claims more assertively would be dishonest, and no research tooling is connected in this run, so I cannot manufacture the missing evidence. What I have done instead is change *what this artifact asserts*:

| Prior attempts asserted | This attempt asserts |
|---|---|
| The problem is that Bengali translation is **too expensive and too slow** (inherited from IB-001/IOH-001) — a claim that requires market evidence we don't have | The problem is **structurally mis-specified as a price problem**, and I give a first-principles argument for that, which does not depend on unavailable sources |
| One undifferentiated "rights holder" problem | Six candidate root causes, decomposed, with a **single cheap discriminating test** that ranks them |
| Confidence low, with no route out | Confidence medium on the *analysis*, low on the *magnitudes*, plus a **pre-registered 24-interview instrument with thresholds** so Step 05 produces rankable evidence instead of anecdote |

The substantive new contribution is §4. It contradicts a load-bearing assumption in IOH-001 and, if correct, prevents us from spending the $8k discovery budget answering the wrong question.

---

## 1. The problem statement (canonical form)

> **An organization that owns English-language content and has a stated Bengali-speaking audience it wants to reach cannot get a Bengali edition of that content produced, published, and demonstrably read — not primarily because translation is expensive, but because the project is *unverifiable* (they cannot judge Bengali quality or cultural fitness themselves), *unquantifiable* (they cannot forecast or later evidence any reader outcome), and *unroutable* (there is no obvious, payable path from a finished Bengali file to actual Bengali readers). Facing three unhedgeable risks at once, they do not commission a cheaper Bengali edition — they commission none at all, indefinitely.**

**The compressed, testable form:**

> Content owners with a Bengali audience mandate **do not commission Bengali editions at any price**, because the deliverable is an unverifiable good with no measurable outcome and no route to market.

**The desired customer outcome, in the customer's own terms:**

> *"I want the Bengali version of this title in front of my Bengali audience inside one programme cycle, at a cost I can defend to my funder or my own P&L, in language my Bengali stakeholders will not embarrass me over, with numbers I can put in a report to prove people actually read it."*

Three verbs, in this order: **verified, delivered, evidenced.** "Translated" is an intermediate step the customer does not care about and cannot evaluate.

---

## 2. Who has this problem

Step 04 owns the full ICP. This step names the **primary problem-holder** so the problem is specific, per the gate criteria.

**DECISION D-004 (PM-001, made autonomously this run): the primary problem-holder for PS-001 is the *reach-motivated institutional content owner*.**

| | Primary problem-holder | Secondary (parallel probe) | Deliberately deferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who | Programme, communications or publications lead inside an NGO, foundation, health/literacy programme, faith publisher, or open-education body that has a **named Bangladesh or West Bengal programme or audience** | Owner of institutional learning content (EdTech, corporate L&D, courseware) needing Bengali for a specific contract, cohort or market | International self-published/mid-list author (IB-001 Segment B) |
| Buys | Reach and defensibility | Coverage and compliance | Revenue and vanity-reach |
| Currency | USD/GBP/EUR, budgeted, often grant-ringfenced | USD/EUR, procurement-driven | USD, personal, discretionary |
| Why primary | Immune to Dhaka/Kolkata price anchoring (mitigates IOH risk R-03/A7); has a pre-existing mandate, so the *need* does not have to be created, only the *route*; recurring content pipeline | Same pipeline, larger and recurring wallet (IOH's H3); cheap to probe in the same motion | See §4.3 — Bengali plausibly fails a rational ROI test for this buyer regardless of our price. Testing them first risks falsifying our *price* thesis while learning nothing about the *real* problem |

**Counter-evidence I am carrying against my own choice (ASSUMPTION, unverified):** the same institutions most likely to have a Bengali mandate are also the most likely to have a **Bangladesh country office or local implementing partner** who will translate in-house at local rates. If so, the primary problem-holder's alternative is not a $9k Western agency but a $400 field-office job — and IOH-001's price advantage evaporates against exactly the segment it named safest. **This is the highest-value single question in Step 05 discovery** and is question Q4 in §9.2.

---

## 3. Problem decomposition — six candidate root causes

The step-03 job is to find *the* problem, not a plausible one. Below are the mutually distinguishable reasons a Bengali edition does not get commissioned, with my hypothesized weight. **The weights are hypotheses, not findings.**

| ID | Root cause | Mechanism | Hypothesized weight | My confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P1** | **Price too high** | Conventional translation cost exceeds expected value of a Bengali edition | 15% | Low — this is IB/IOH's central thesis and I think it is over-weighted |
| **P2** | **Return unquantifiable** | Buyer cannot forecast readers, downloads, or impact, so *no* price is justifiable because the denominator is unknown. A $200 edition is still unbuyable if you cannot say what it achieves | **25%** | Medium |
| **P3** | **Quality unverifiable** | Buyer does not read Bengali. Cannot inspect the deliverable, cannot distinguish good from fluent-but-wrong, and carries **reputational** downside if a native stakeholder criticizes it. Unhedgeable information asymmetry → default to inaction | **25%** | Medium-High |
| **P4** | **No route to reader** | Even with a perfect Bengali file, the buyer has no distribution, no discovery, no local payment rail, no marketing into Bangladesh/West Bengal. The output is a file, not reach | **20%** | Medium |
| **P5** | **Coordination cost** | The project needs 5–7 coordinated vendors (translator, native editor, proofreader, typesetter/Indic typography, cover, metadata, distributor) in an unfamiliar language and market. Transaction and attention cost exceeds expected value even if each part is cheap | 10% | Medium |
| **P6** | **Rights friction** | Translation rights sit with a trade publisher unwilling to sublicense a "small" language, or the work is multi-party | 5% for the primary holder (usually owns its own content); high for Segment B mid-list authors | Medium |

**INFERENCE (the structural argument, independent of market data):** P1 is the only root cause our current product thesis (cheap, fast translation + production) directly attacks. P2, P3 and P4 together carry a hypothesized **70%** of the blockage. If that ranking is even roughly right, we could hit IOH-001's $1,500/3-week target perfectly and still record zero sales — and IOH's kill trigger K2 ("<3 paid invoices") would fire while telling us nothing about *why*. **A problem statement built on P1 alone is the single most expensive mistake available to us at this step.**

---
